item.research_question: How can electrical homogeneity be achieved in BiFeO3–BaTiO3 (BF–BT) based ceramics to eliminate conductive pathways and enhance breakdown strength and energy storage density?
item.material_system: BiFeO3–BaTiO3 (BF–BT) bulk and multilayer ceramics, specifically doped with 8 mol % Nd(Zr0.5Zn0.5)O3 (NZZ) and the system BF–ST–xNb–yBMN
item.processing_route: Solid-state reaction route to produce bulk ceramics; fabrication of multilayer (ML) structures; doping with NZZ or donor doping with Nb on the B-site; sintering in appropriate atmospheres to control oxygen stoichiometry
item.test_conditions: Electric fields up to 700 kV cm–1 for bulk and 700 kV cm–1 for MLs; temperature range from room temperature to 250 °C; frequency range 0.1 to 100 Hz; impedance spectroscopy (IS) performed at room temperature and 660 °C
key_findings: Undoped 0.7BF–0.3BT ceramics exhibited two electrical components with vastly different resistances (R1 ~ 3.8 kΩ cm and R2 ~ 1.3 MΩ cm), leading to breakdown at lower fields.
Doping with 8 mol % NZZ eliminated the conductive component, resulting in a single electrical component with resistivity ~2.3 MΩ cm.
Optimized Wrec of 2.45 J cm–3 was realized at Emax ~ 240 kV cm–1 for 0.08NZZ-BF–BT bulk ceramics.
Optimized Wrec of 10.5 J cm–3 was realized at Emax ~ 700 kV cm–1 for 0.08NZZ-BF–BT multilayer ceramics.
In BF–ST–xNb–yBMN ceramics, Nb doping suppressed Fe4+ formation and reduced electrical conductivity by several orders of magnitude.
At x = 0.03 Nb, the breakdown strength increased to 360 kV cm–1.
Combining 0.03 Nb with 0.1 BMN resulted in Wrec ~ 8.2 J cm–3 at Emax ~ 460 kV cm–1.
The Seebeck coefficient decreased from ~600 μV K–1 to zero as Nb concentration increased, indicating a decrease in charge carrier concentration.
item.mechanism: Electrical heterogeneity in BF–BT ceramics arises from conductive cores (low resistance) and resistive shells/grain boundaries, creating pathways for breakdown. Alloying with a third end-member (NZZ) or donor doping (Nb) suppresses the formation of oxygen vacancies and Fe4+ species, thereby eliminating the conductive component and creating an electrically homogeneous microstructure with high resistivity, which allows the material to withstand higher electric fields without breakdown.
item.limitations: The text notes that for BF-based ceramics, the defect chemistry of cores and shells remains to be fully elucidated and that initial work suggests further dopants are needed to create electrical homogeneity.
item.future_work: The authors propose that future development requires strategies to optimize energy storage by controlling local structure, phase assemblage, dielectric layer thickness, microstructure, conductivity, and electrical homogeneity through the choice of base systems, dopants, and alloying additions.
quotes: Electrical heterogeneity was effectively eliminated by alloying with a third end-member so that it became more difficult to form a conductive pathway at high field, resulting in higher BDS and Wrec.
The conductive electrical component was effectively eliminated by forming a solid solution with NZZ, inhibiting the formation of conductive pathways at higher electric field (>500 kV cm–1).

Nb doping suppresses the formation of Fe4+ associated with the loss of Bi2O3 or/and VO.. during ceramic processing, thus reducing electrical conductivity with respect to x = 0 by several orders of magnitude.

item.research_question: How do annealing parameters, glass matrix composition, and novel processing methods (e.g., microwave treatment) influence the crystallization, microstructure, and energy storage properties (Wrec, BDS) of glass-ceramics?
item.material_system: Na2O–BaO–SrO–Nb2O5–SiO2–B2O3, BaO–PbO–Na2O–Nb2O5–SiO2–Al2O3 (BPNN-AS), SrO–Na2O–Nb2O5–SiO2, K2O–BaO–Nb2O5–SiO2, SrO–BaO–K2O–Nb2O5–SiO2, BaO–R2O–Nb2O5–SiO2 (R=Li, Na, K), BaO–B2O3–Al2O3–SiO2, SrO–BaO–Nb2O5–SiO2–Al2O3, BaO–SrO–TiO2–Al2O3–SiO2, SrO–BaO–Nb2O5–B2O3–ZnO, BaO–SrO–TiO2–Al2O3–B2O3–SiO2, BaxSr1-xTiO3−(Ba−B−Al−Si−O), K2O–SrO–Nb2O5–SiO2–Al2O3–B2O3
item.processing_route: Melting raw materials, cooling to room temperature to form a glass, followed by two-step annealing: nucleation at approximately the glass transition temperature (Tg) and crystal growth at temperatures > Tg. Microwave treatment was also used to restrain dendritic microstructure formation.
item.test_conditions: Energy storage properties evaluated via P-E loops and discharging processes; crystallization temperatures ranged from 800 °C to 1000 °C; annealing times varied (e.g., 10 min for microwave sintering).
key_findings: Wang and co-workers reported an ultrahigh Wrec of 20.7 J cm–3 in BPNN-AS glass ceramics at an optimized crystallization temperature of 900 °C.
In BPNN-AS, increasing crystallization temperature from 850 to 1000 °C decreased BDS from 1890 to 1440 kV cm–1 while crystallinity increased from 64.5 to 97.3%.
Chen and co-workers obtained a remarkably high BDS of ~1400 kV cm–1 with εr of ~50, leading to a Wrec of 4 J cm–3 in Na2O–BaO–SrO–Nb2O5–SiO2–B2O3 glass ceramics at 800 °C.
For SrO–Na2O–Nb2O5–SiO2 glass ceramics, the optimal εr of 120 and BDS of ~1700 kV cm–1 were obtained with 35 mol % SiO2, resulting in a theoretical Wrec of 15.2 J cm–3.
Substitution of Sr for Ba in SrO–BaO–K2O–Nb2O5–SiO2 led to a highest BDS of ~1800 kV cm–1 and Wrec of 17.5 J cm–3 with Sr = 0.4.
Liu and co-workers achieved a highest Wrec of ~19 J cm–3 with εr of ~22 and a superior BDS of ~4400 kV cm–1 in BaO–Na2O–K2O–Nb2O5–SiO2 glass ceramics.
Zhang and co-workers found that microwave treatment improved BDS from 1200 kV cm–1 to 1500 kV cm–1 in BST-BBAS glass-ceramics, corresponding to a Wrec of 2.8 J cm–3.
Smith and co-workers reported both ultrahigh Emax of ~12000 kV cm–1 and Wrec of ~35 J cm–3 in BaO–B2O3–Al2O3–SiO2 glass.
item.mechanism: The high BDS and Wrec are attributed to the absence of 2D and 3D defects (e.g., grain boundaries) in the largely defect-free glass phase and the uniform distribution of the ceramic phase. The volume fraction of the crystalline phase increases with annealing temperature and time, which increases εr but decreases BDS; thus, optimized Wrec is a balance between εr and BDS. Rare-earth oxides act as nucleating agents or crystal growth inhibitors to achieve homogeneous microstructures and reduce crystallite size.
item.limitations: Generally, increasing the volume fraction of the crystal phase increases εr but decreases BDS. The mechanism of crystallization and control of crystal phase/microstructure is still ambiguous. Although theoretical Wrec (>15 J cm–3) is high due to ultrahigh BDS, measured/calculated Wrec by P-E loops is low (<2 J cm–3) due to lower applied electric fields.
item.future_work: The mechanism of crystallization and control of crystal phase/microstructure should be further investigated using advanced TEM and in situ XRD/TEM as a function of applied field and temperature. The authors recommend using the same test method (P-E loops and discharging process) to evaluate the practical energy storage performance for glass-ceramics, consistent with other dielectrics.
quotes: Wrec and η are both large due to the high BDS associated with the absence of 2D and 3D defects accompanied by a near zero value of Pr.
The optimized Wrec is a balance between εr and BDS.

The mechanism of crystallization and control of crystal phase/microstructure is still ambiguous, which should be further investigated using, advanced TEM and in situ XRD/TEM as a function of applied field and temperature.
